The +1 hand damage is offset by the 1 damage the card deals (make sure
you have ANI) which is unpreventable. IG is useless if they maneuver to
long range. In fact, a DoTB/IG combo is basically saying, "sit still
while I punch you and there's *nothing* you can do about it." (lousy
fortitude...) And then there's Song of Serenity to take back that 1
hand damage. All in all, an ani/pot combat deck without DoTB is a bad
ani/pot combat deck. In cel/pot decks, you get Flash and stuff for
maneuvering. While not as good as DoTB, Flash is necessary. In ani/pot
you have no maneuvers. But a single DoTB keeps them from playing how
ever many maneuvers they might have (and keeps them from cycling cards,
too).

-Chris

other pot-combat decks - pot/pro, or pot/for?? especially
with DotB. "here, we'll fight at close range and you can

they're pot/for. dont' get me wrong, it's not a BAD card...
but I dont' see it as being as key a card as say, IG.

combat decks... DotB is just fine against Tha, or non-combat

Messages.Author: Jasper Phillips
Messages.Body:
In article <367073f2...@news.mindspring.com>,

William Pyle <wp...@mindspring.com> wrote:
>I've got a strategy question....
>
>what makes DotB a good card? I can't remember who or
>where specifically, but everyone seems to think this is a good
>card for a combat deck. ok, it limits your opponent to pretty
>much letting you set the range to close, and keeps em
>from using equipment.

[snip 8<]

One of the main problems in a close range combat deck is how
many maneuvers to include. Too many and you'll hand clog, too
few, and they'll never do you any good. DotB completely trumps
your opponent's maneuver attempts, no matter how many he plays,
and can be freely cycled in any combat. The flexibility in deck
construction and play this allows is huge. In practice the extra damage
you take often doesn't matter, as you can play Taste of Vitae
to allow for it, and if you're facing another potence deck the one
point of damage difference won't likely matter.

Of course, it's not such a clear cut case, as that extra damage
can be a pain, and it's easier to build crypts out of vampires with
pot/cel or pot/obf than pot/ani. In general I tend to like DotB best
when it's combined with either Fortitude, or Hidden Lurker (decks
that use such things often have larger vampires anyway, for one thing).

--

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
William Pyle wrote:
"what makes DotB a good card? I can't remember who or
where specifically, but everyone seems to think this is a good
card for a combat deck. ok, it limits your opponent to pretty
much letting you set the range to close, and keeps em
from using equipment."

To throw in without being too redundant, DotB is a good card because it makes
your strategy work. If you are building a close range, Immortal Grapple based
combat deck, you _need_ to be at close range, or your deck is pointless. You
have three options:

1. Hope your opponents don't manuver. This is sketchy and will get you killed.

2. Use your own manuvers. This is a good option for Cel or Pro based decks,
cause they have multi purpose manuver cards and thus are less likely to find
themselves with either too many or too few manuver cards. Other disciplines
(like Obf) have a bit more trouble with their less versitile manuvers, as it is
really important to have them, but if you don't need them (cause your opponents
don't manuver), they are difficult to cycle and can jam your hand if you have
too many, but you might never draw them when you need them if you have too few.

3. Use DotB. You can always play DotB, regardless of what your opponent does
(i.e. it will never jam your hand), it completely prevents your opponent from
doing what he wants to do (i.e. manuver away), and makes your deck work the way
it is supposed to (i.e. you are always at close range).

Yes, it gives your opponent extra +1 hand damage, which makes a bit of
difference against, say, the Gangrel, but if you don't have For, the Gangrel
are going to kill you anyway. Against non combat decks, DotB will be always
useful, and the extra damage won't make any difference (as you can play Taste
to get the blood back). Against long range combat decks, the extra hand damage
won't matter, as you will be denying them their main strategy, and you will
have the combat advantage, as you are using yours. Against other close range
combat decks, you don't have to play the DotB, so it is moot.

That, and there is the mythical "All DotB/Form of Mist" deck that gets into
combat, plays N+1 DotB (where N = the amount of blood on the opposing vampire)
at superior, and then plays Strike: Combat Ends to send the opposing vampire to
torpor with no possible way to avoid it. Very similar to the "All Weather
Control, All the Time" deck of legend.

I'm failing to see your confusion, as you have answered your own question
pretty well. If your opponents are playing other close range combat decks, you
have zero need to play DotB. If they want to hit you with hand damage, and you
want to hit them with hand damage, why would you bother playing DotB against
them? You are correct. You wouldn't. If you are in an environement with lots
of close range combat, do yourself a favor and take out all of your DotB. If
your opponents are playing ranged combat decks (Brujah Pitch, Tremere, some
sort of gun deck), DotB makes you win. If your opponents are playing non
combat decks that may or may not have manuvers for combat avoidance, DotB makes
you win. If your opponents are playing the same sort of deck you are
(presumably close range combat), then DotB is not needed, so you either neglect
to put them in your deck or you play them for the extra point of unpreventable
damage and to keep them from pressing to end (if you aren't going to get
killed).

William Pyle wrote:
"do you guys (anyone) play a kinda sideboard-type setup? we usually do, so we
can (but usually end up not bothering to) tweak our decks a little depending on
what everyone's playing..."

Nah. Generally most players I have run across (as well as myself) find
"sideboarding" for Jyhad to be pretty contrary to the basic game concept. As
opposed to Magic which is far more about "card vs card" (or, say, Star Wars
which is about nothing _but_ "card vs card"), Jyhad is a game of "strategy vs
strategy". Jyhad is about how Rush works against Stealth and Bleed or how
Intercept works against Vote, not how card A can beat up card B. That, and
sideboarding makes the anti-clan masters _way_ more powerful than they should
be (anti-clan masters generally have very powerful effects that are balanced
out by their extreme opportunity cost).

Not to say that you are a bad person if your group likes sideboards. If it
makes you happy, go with it. However, sideboards aren't a part of actual
competetive Jyhad, and I don't think many folks use it them in general.

On the other hand, a real important part of the game of Jyhad is "The Meta
Game" (a phrase thrown about left and right around here), which generally
refers to the evolution of decks between play sessions, rather than between
hands. It works sort of the same way, but it is more of a "Hmm, there are lots
of combat decks around here. How do I build a deck to do well in an
environment with lots of combat decks?" sort of evolution than a "Hmm. Josh is
playing with the Tremere tonight. I'd better get out my Letters from Vienna"
sort of thing (as well as being more guesswork, as you don't really know what
deck the guy next to you is going to be playing anyway--you have to work with
trends and favored strategies, rather than concrete knowledge). For example,
around here (long, long ago...), I discovered that Immortal Grapple made for
really good combat decks, so I started playing effective, killer combat decks.
This started a horrible combat deck arms race, and so to stay ahead of the
curve, I developed a really nasty Potence/Fortitude combat deck, that kept
beating all the other combat decks. Then someone got sick of being killed by
stupid combat decks, and made a completely anti-combat bleed deck, and kicked
all of our assess. Thus, the combat deck players had to put together non
combat decks to compete with the anti-combat decks, and so on. This didn't
happen between hands, it happened between gaming sessions, so there were
completely new decks at every game.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
pd...@aol.com (PDB6) wrote:
> Yeah, hey. What is the current state of interaction between WWEF and Mind
Numb
> or that "You can't untap" card?

As allowed by card text. Generally, this means that Wake is usable and
operates as normal. The "doesn't untap" cards are usually "as normal during
the untap phase" - which allows untapping by other means, and certainly
allows waking, which doesn't actually untap the vampire at all. Mind Numb
falls in this category.

That "You can't untap" card is Sleeping Mind. In the inferior it will
defeat the as-yet-unplayed Wakey if the vampire that would've been woken
is the on selected by Sleeping Mind.

In the superior, it does not restrict waking (although it does restrict
untap effects like Rat's Warning), since Wake doesn't actually untap the
vampire.

--
